analysis.one_liner: Narrows which streams and wetlands the Clean Water Act protects and repeals the 2015 water rule.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action after being referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in July 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the 2015 Clean Water Rule and write a much narrower definition of 'navigable waters' directly into law. Only territorial seas, interstate commercial waters, permanent streams and lakes that flow into them, and wetlands visibly connected to those waters would count; intermittent streams, groundwater, drained farmland, ditches, irrigation systems, prior converted cropland, and water-filled depressions from mining or construction would be excluded. It would also let landowners get a free, binding federal decision on whether water on their land is regulated, due within 60 days — with silence meaning it is not regulated [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers, landowners, homebuilders, mining companies, and energy developers. The narrower definition removes federal permitting requirements over many ditches, drained fields, seasonal streams, and mining ponds, and the binding-determination process gives them a quick, cost-free answer when they are unsure whether a permit is needed [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farmers, developers, mining and energy companies

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 2015 Clean Water Rule and replaces it with a statutory definition, ending a contested regulatory back-and-forth over which waters are federally protected [S2][S3].

Excludes intermittent and ephemeral streams, groundwater including tiled drainage, ditches and irrigation systems, prior converted cropland, and water-filled depressions from mining or construction from federal jurisdiction [S3].

Creates a binding jurisdictional-determination process: the Secretary of the Army must answer a landowner's request within 60 days at federal cost, and if no answer comes, the waters are deemed not regulated; a 'non-navigable' finding is binding for as long as the owner holds the property [S3].
Allows expedited judicial review of those determinations in federal district court within 30 days [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Downstream communities and the general public. Smaller and seasonal streams and disconnected-looking wetlands feed the rivers and aquifers that supply drinking water, absorb floodwater, and filter pollution; removing them from federal protection would leave their condition to state rules of varying strength, and pollution upstream would surface downstream at someone else's expense [S3].

drawbacks.text: Ephemeral and intermittent streams — explicitly excluded by the bill — feed the larger rivers that carry drinking water, so pollution released into a dry streambed can reach public water supplies downstream [S3].

Wetlands without a visually obvious surface connection still absorb floods and filter runoff; the bill's requirement of a 'continuous surface water connection' an ordinary person could see with the naked eye would strip protection from many of them [S3].

Specific carve-outs — drain tiling, irrigation and drainage systems, and water-filled depressions incidental to mining or construction — would remove federal review of some of the pathways by which farm and mine runoff enters shared waters [S3].
The bill would apply the new definition by statute, making it harder for future administrations to restore broader protections through regulation [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does offer something real: landowners get a fast, free, binding answer about whether they need a federal permit, and everyone gets a fixed statutory definition after years of rule changes and litigation. But the definition is drawn broadly in favor of exempting seasonal streams, drained farmland, and mining and construction depressions, and the protections those waters provide downstream — cleaner drinking water, flood absorption, pollution filtering — would be lost. The cost falls on people downstream who had no say in the upstream land use.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in July 2019, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Braun introduced the bill with Sen. Joni Ernst as cosponsor on July 31, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1][S3][S4].
No further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — was ever recorded before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it never advanced, Clean Water Act jurisdiction was not narrowed by statute, so downstream communities and drinking-water users keep the existing protections. Landowners and developers continue to face the same regulatory uncertainty the bill was written to end.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Republicans and no Democrats signed on; there was never a vote to reveal any broader split.

industries.note: The bill excludes prior converted cropland, tiled subsurface drainage, ditches, and irrigation systems from federal jurisdiction, sparing farm operations from Clean Water Act permitting. Runoff from those features reaches shared waters, so the cost of lighter oversight lands on downstream users.

Excluding seasonal streams, wetlands without a visible surface connection, and stormwater and construction depressions would remove federal permitting hurdles over land development. Fewer federal reviews means wetlands and headwaters that absorb floods and filter water go unprotected.
Water-filled depressions created in upland, including those incidental to mining or construction, would be exempt from federal jurisdiction, easing one permitting constraint on those operations.

The binding, free 60-day jurisdictional determination — with non-response counting as non-regulated — is a genuine benefit to any property owner unsure of their obligations, regardless of industry. The benefit is procedural certainty rather than environmental protection.
